newsitem.title: PERU: Angry Peruvians demand solution to hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Angry Peruvians demand solution to hostage crisis.

text.p: Angry and embarrassed at the week-old siege of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, Peruvians are becoming increasingly impatient with their government's failure to find a solution to the crisis.

A few favour military intervention, and another minority would like the government to continue wearing down the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels while refusing them any sort of olive branch.
But most Peruvians now appear to back a negotiated solution to secure the freedom of the remaining 105 hostages and end a crisis that is costing their country dearly.

"They (the rebels) have already ruined our Christmas and blackened Peru's name on every front page in the world. We shouldn't let them spoil New Year as well," said street-cleaner Cesar Grados, working two blocks from the besieged residence. "The government has to solve this, and fast."

He supported the idea of paying off the rebels, then offering them exile abroad -- possibly Cuba from where they draw their ideology or Ecuador which has offered to help -- or giving them safe passage to the jungle zone they came from.
None, it seems, want the government to give in to the rebels' principal demand -- the freedom of jailed comrades.
"I am totally opposed to an exchange deal -- the hostages for the prisoners," said taxi driver Braulio Garcia.

"Not one of those miserable killers should be let out of jail. If they let even a few of them out, it opens the way for other groups to use similar tactics, and it would send us back to another decade of terrorism."

President Alberto Fujimori has flatly ruled out that option, while the MRTA has said it will not release the government-linked hostages, who form the majority of the remaining captives, unless their imprisoned comrades are freed.

"We are waiting for the government to do something. But Fujimori has only spoken publicly once," said Jonny Rojas, a policeman with Peru's Special Operations on guard outside the residence. "If it was up to us, we'd just go in there and blow them up. They must be tired by now. We could catch them off guard."

Another Taxi driver, Alberto Rojas, agreed. "Police should go in and liquidate the lot of them," he said. "If we lose 50 or 100 hostages, that's still better than another 15 years of terrorism which is what we get if we cave in."

According to police sources, the government has crack troops waiting in the wings if it decides to intervene. But with the avoidance of bloodshed a priority, Fujimori prefers for now not to storm the residence.

Despite his public silence, Fujimori is thought to be mulling a detailed range of options with a small group of his closest advisers. The presence of his brother, Pedro Fujimori, among the hostages has added a personal dimension to what is the biggest dilemma of the president's often tumultuous career.

"Fujimori is a hard man used to taking difficult decisions. But even he will find it hard to send the troops in against such an eminent group of men, including his own brother," said newspaper salesman Abraham Garcia.
"What he should do is let the MRTA members go to Cuba or back to the Huallaga (jungle) with four or five hostages as security for safe passage," Garcia said.

The Peruvian people's impatience was accentuated by their despondence at seeing the country's international reputation dive again just as it began to emerge from the shadows of 16 years of guerrilla conflict.
Bombings, kidnappings and sabotage by the MRTA and the Shining Path, its better known guerrilla group rival, have cost at least 30,000 lives and $25 billion in damage since 1980.
